rationale: Taint-based confirmation and egress allowlists block the data-exfiltration and API-call vectors, but manipulation of the model's text output (misinformation, persuasion, contaminated answers) is not blockable by action-feature rules.

value: Treat all retrieved content (web pages, documents, code, emails) as untrusted data. (1) Taint tracking: after the context has ingested untrusted content, block or require user confirmation for side-effect tool calls (API calls, sending data, rendering links or images with URLs). (2) Egress allowlist: outbound requests and rendered URLs may only go to allowlisted domains, and URLs must not carry data from the context. (3) Do not allow tool calls that untrusted content proposes unless they are in a task-scoped allowlist.

rationale: Indirect injection via untrusted data (web pages, documents, emails retrieved by agent) is mechanically distinguishable from direct user instructions; whitelisting retrieval sources and re-approving embedded directives before API calls blocks the attack vector.

value: Agent must not call APIs or exfiltrate data based on instructions embedded in retrieved data sources unless: (1) those data sources are marked as trusted/curated by the owner, AND (2) the retrieved instruction is re-approved by the owner before execution, OR (3) API call targets and data destinations are whitelisted per data source category at deployment time, blocking new destinations found in embeddings.

rationale: Microsoft deployed Bing Chat; indirect injection exploits legitimate deployment
Executing model-generated code with eval in the host process is a static, checkable design flaw that a sandbox or AST allowlist blocks without hurting the math task.

value: Tool 'python_eval'/code-exec must never run in the host process: execute only in a sandbox (no network, no filesystem outside scratch, no host secrets, CPU/time limits), or use a restricted expression parser (AST allowlist of arithmetic nodes) instead of eval/exec. Deny any eval/exec on LLM-generated strings in the host interpreter.

rationale: Arbitrary code execution is preventable by restricting the evaluator's capabilities at deployment time; this is a standard sandbox pattern, not context-dependent.

value: LLMMathChain must not execute user-supplied Python code directly. All math evaluations must use a sandboxed expression evaluator (e.g., ast.literal_eval, sympy.sympify, numexpr) that rejects function definitions, imports, and attribute access. Code execution is prohibited at the action level regardless of LLM reasoning.

rationale: Deployer chose LangChain math chain design; architecture allows arbitrary code execution via eval
Image-URL exfiltration and cross-plugin calls after untrusted input are blockable by egress allowlist and taint-based approval gates, but the general class of injected instructions is not solved.

value: (1) Output filter: block markdown images/links whose URL host is not on an allowlist or whose URL query/path contains content derived from session context. (2) Taint rule: once a tool result from an untrusted source (web page) enters context, any call to a different plugin/tool with side effects or outbound data requires explicit user approval. (3) Per-plugin least-privilege scopes.

rationale: The first-order harm (unauthorized plugin chaining) is blockable by approval gates on resource scope; exfiltration via markdown is harder because legitimate markdown can be used in legitimate contexts.

value: Plugin invocation must require explicit per-action approval when: (a) the action's target resource is not directly named in the user's current request, or (b) the action would read/write data outside the user's intended scope. Cross-plugin data flows (output of one plugin fed as input to another without user request) must be blocked or require approval.

rationale: Deployer integrated plugins without egress/taint gates; architecture allows cross-plugin leakage
Sandbox isolation with read-only config and no host mounts blocks the container-to-host escape regardless of the injection, even in continuous mode.

value: Agent code/shell execution must run in an isolated container with no writes to its own config, Dockerfile, entrypoint or mounted host paths, and no host mounts or docker socket. Autonomous/continuous mode must not disable approval for file writes to agent config or code, and for execution of files the agent has written. Deny writes to the agent's own source/config/startup files.

rationale: Host RCE via container reconfiguration is blockable by filtering system-level commands and enforcing approval gates; removing the gate in 'continuous mode' was an oversight control, not a first-order harm prevention.

value: Code execution tools must reject: (a) shell commands that modify container/host configuration (setuid, mount, chroot, restart daemons, write to /etc or /sys), (b) commands that reach beyond the container boundary (host filesystem mounts, docker.sock access). Additionally, any approved shell execution must remain gated by per-action approval, never disabled in 'continuous' mode without explicit whitelist of safe operations.

rationale: Deployer removed per-step approval in continuous mode; lacked container sandbox and read-only config
The exfiltration channel is an image URL fetched by the client, which a domain allowlist or disabling external image rendering closes.

value: Rendered output must not load remote images or links from non-allowlisted domains (Content-Security-Policy img-src allowlist, or strip markdown images with external URLs). Block any outbound URL containing query strings or path data from conversation context.

rationale: Preventing image URLs from carrying exfiltrated data is checkable: audit all URL generation to block user-data parameters and restrict external URL sources in output.

value: Any image URL emitted by the agent must be whitelisted or generated by the agent itself. If an image URL is derived from external sources (web pages, documents, user input), it must not contain or be rewritten to contain user data (session tokens, chat history, personal identifiers). External URLs in agent output are prohibited unless explicitly requested by the user to fetch a specific URL.

rationale: Deployer integrated external image rendering; architecture lacks URL allowlist and no egress gate
Markdown-image exfiltration is mechanically blocked by egress allowlisting on rendering, independent of the injected text.

value: Rendered assistant output must not auto-fetch images or links from non-allowlisted domains (CSP img-src allowlist or strip external markdown images). Deny output URLs whose query/path carries content copied from private documents.

rationale: Preventing document exfiltration via URL parameters is a concrete, checkable rule: audit URL generation logic to disallow user-data encoding.

value: Image URLs emitted by the agent must not be constructed from, include, or reference user-uploaded documents, chat history, or private workspace data. All image URLs must either be generated/hosted by the platform or must be whitelisted external URLs with no dynamic parameters derived from user data.

rationale: Deployer deployed assistant without egress allowlist; markdown-image exfiltration channel unblocked
GitHub fixed it by disabling markdown image rendering, which a standard egress-allowlist rule would have done up front.

value: Chat UI must not render markdown images or other auto-fetched resources from non-allowlisted domains (CSP img-src limited to the vendor's own domains). Block rendered URLs that embed chat or code context in query/path.

rationale: Disabling markdown image rendering or enforcing URL sanitization is a standard content-security pattern; it blocks the exfiltration vector without breaking legitimate chat.

value: Markdown image syntax (![alt](url)) must be stripped from agent output or rendered locally only. External image URLs must not be generated from agent reasoning. If markdown rendering is enabled, all image URLs must be sanitized to disallow: (a) dynamic parameters, (b) user data encoding, (c) cross-origin requests that carry session context.

rationale: Deployer shipped Copilot with markdown image rendering enabled; no egress allowlist configured
Unsandboxed exec() of LLM-generated code is a generic, checkable anti-pattern, so a sandbox or no-exec rule blocks the RCE.

value: Code generated by an LLM must not be executed in the host process (no exec/eval). Run it only in a sandbox with no network, no filesystem access outside a scratch directory, and no credentials. Alternatively, accept only a whitelisted declarative chart spec instead of code. Require human approval for any generated-code execution outside the sandbox.

rationale: Code execution is irreversible and high-risk; a standard pre-deployment spec for text-to-code systems would mandate showing generated code before execution, blocking this injection vector entirely.

value: Before executing any generated code (SQL, Python, shell, or other), require explicit human approval of the code text. Do not auto-execute visualizations that require code generation without displaying the code and awaiting confirmation.

rationale: Deployer enabled visualization with unsandboxed exec(); no-exec or sandbox rule absent from architecture
Exfiltration channels and egress after taint can be gated mechanically, but the general class of injected instructions and in-context spear-phishing text cannot be fully blocked.

value: Taint tracking: once untrusted content (external email, shared docs) enters the context, block or require approval for outbound actions. These include drafting or sending email to recipients not named by the user, rendering links or images with data in the URL, and any retrieval from sources outside the user's current request. Block URLs whose domain is outside an allowlist. Apply a sensitivity-label filter that excludes credential-pattern content from retrieval.

rationale: Auto-invocation of tools on injected content is blockable. However, once tools execute, surfacing existing credentials/data is a concealment/disclosure problem harder to prevent purely by constraint.

value: Block tool invocations on untrusted input (messages from external users, public channels, forwarded content). Require explicit user action to invoke tools; do not auto-invoke based on message content alone.

rationale: Deployer integrated without egress gating or taint-based tool access; design lacks mechanical blocks
The markdown-link exfiltration channel and taint-based retrieval mixing are checkable, but whether a secret is sensitive is context-dependent, and the injection itself is not detectable.

value: Retrieval must enforce the access scope of the requesting user and of the content's origin. Once the context contains content authored by a user who is not the requester, block rendering of links with data-bearing URLs (non-allowlisted domains). Do not mix private-channel content into answers when the context contains public, attacker-writable content, unless the user approves.

rationale: A constraint blocking disclosure of data from inaccessible resources is writable and would catch the cross-channel leak. However, detecting whether a resource is 'secret' vs. already-known is contextual; the constraint only blocks disclosure, not the initial access.

value: Require explicit approval gate before returning information from access-controlled resources (private channels, restricted folders). Flag all content sourced from resources the invoking user does not explicitly have read access to.

rationale: Deployer configured retrieval without taint tracking or cross-channel access control; no egress gate
Taint-based tool gating and egress URL allowlisting are standard rules that block both the automatic search and the hidden-link exfiltration.

value: When the context contains content from an external or untrusted sender (inbound email), disable automatic tool invocation (mailbox search, file search). Require explicit user approval for any further retrieval. Render no hyperlinks or images whose URL contains retrieved data or points to a non-allowlisted domain.

rationale: Auto-search on injected email instructions is entirely preventable by requiring user approval before tool use. This is standard practice in pre-deployment specs for email agents.

value: Do not auto-invoke search or fetch tools based on injected content. Require explicit user confirmation before tool invocation; in particular, do not search for or retrieve data in response to instructions embedded in user-visible messages (emails, chat).

rationale: Deployer enabled automatic tool invocation without taint-based gating; no egress allowlist configured
A taint-conditioned memory-write gate plus an egress allowlist blocks both the persistence and the exfiltration steps.

value: Memory writes need user confirmation, or are blocked, when untrusted content (web pages, documents, tool outputs) is in the context. Memory entries may not contain instructions to send, forward, or encode conversation data. Block rendering of image or link URLs to non-allowlisted domains, and block any network request that includes conversation content.

rationale: Blocking auto-write to memory/state on untrusted input is writable and would prevent the initial injection. However, detecting whether a future message is 'leaking' is a separate concealment problem not fully solvable by action constraints.

value: Do not allow memory-write or state-mutation tools to be auto-invoked based on user message content. Require explicit user confirmation before persisting instructions or state that will affect future conversations.

rationale: Deployer shipped memory tool with auto-invocation and no taint gate; egress allowlist absent
Download-then-execute and egress to unknown hosts are observable command features that a standard computer-use safety spec would gate.

value: Run the agent in a sandbox VM with no host credentials and with network egress limited to an allowlist. Block downloading and executing binaries or scripts from non-allowlisted origins. Require human approval for any shell command that executes a file downloaded in the same session, or that opens an outbound connection to a non-allowlisted host.

rationale: Binary execution without approval is entirely preventable. Any pre-deployment safety spec for host-access agents would mandate explicit approval-before-execute for downloaded binaries and system commands.

value: Before executing any binary or running any command-line tool on a host, require explicit human approval and display the full invocation (binary path, arguments, source). Do not execute downloaded or remotely-sourced binaries without user consent on a per-action basis.

rationale: Deployer ran agent autonomously in reference demo; no download-execute gate or egress allowlist
A taint-based gate on memory writes blocks this vector, but the general class of injected instructions that look legitimate is not fully closed.

value: Writes to long-term memory require explicit user confirmation, and are blocked in any turn whose context includes untrusted external content (uploaded documents, web pages, emails). Memory writes carry a provenance tag, and memory written from untrusted-tainted turns is never auto-loaded as trusted instructions.

rationale: Injection vector (untrusted doc) is blockable via approval gating, but persistent poisoning itself is harder—a rule blocks *injection-triggered* writes but not user-approved false memories.

value: Memory write operations must be limited to facts explicitly confirmed by user action (button click, explicit approval) in the current conversation turn. Reject memory updates triggered solely by passive document content or model inference of user intent.

rationale: Legitimate user ran Gemini; untrusted document injected malicious instructions
Cross-origin data-flow and egress rules block this exfiltration path, but confirmation prompts were bypassed in the demo, and the general injection class stays open.

value: Block form submissions and text entry to any domain other than the one the user named for the task. Block pasting of data read from one origin into a different origin. Require a user-confirmation token, given outside the page content, for any submission of personal-profile fields to a third-party origin.

rationale: Injected content can bypass UI prompts, but a *mandatory hold point* before sensitive I/O (clipboard write) is mechanically enforceable and would stop the exfiltration.

value: Before executing any clipboard/form-fill action on a third-party domain, the agent must display the data being pasted to the user and await explicit confirmation. Clipboard operations must never execute silently or proceed past a user confirmation prompt.

rationale: User ran Operator; site injection bypassed security confirmations
Hidden-character filtering and diff flagging block this vector, but other visible or semantically subtle backdoors in rules files still pass.

value: Reject or strip invisible and bidirectional Unicode characters (zero-width, bidi controls, tag characters) from rules and config files before they enter the agent context. Flag any generated diff that adds new network calls, new dependencies, or external script includes for mandatory human review.

rationale: Injected rules are checkable via output attribution and version hashes. Rule does not block code generation, but forces transparency—user review becomes informed rather than passive.

value: Code generation suggestions must be tagged with the source of the instructions that produced them (e.g. 'rules-file', 'user-chat', 'system'). If the source is a shared/versioned file, include file hash. Users must review and approve suggestions from non-chat sources before merge.

rationale: Developer ran assistants; shared rules file contained injected backdoor
A private-to-public information-flow rule, plus least-privilege token scoping, blocks the exfiltration without stopping the intended task.

value: Within one session, once the agent has read a private repo or other private resource, block write actions to public targets (public PRs, public issues, public comments). Scope the agent's token to the single repo named in the task (least privilege). Require explicit human approval for any cross-repo read triggered by content from an untrusted issue.

rationale: Issue content cannot be fully sanitized, but repo access scope is a hard architectural boundary. Deny-by-default with explicit allow is standard least-privilege.

value: MCP server tools that access repositories must enforce: (a) explicit user allowlist of accessible repos per session, (b) any repo access outside the allowlist triggers an error halt and user notification, (c) PR/issue creation is restricted to repos on the allowlist. Deny-by-default; repos must be explicitly enabled.

rationale: Legitimate agent ran; malicious public issue injected exfiltration instructions
This is a server-side access-control bug in the MCP tool layer, not an agent action. A tenant-isolation invariant would block it, but it is classic software assurance rather than agent safety.

value: Every data-access call carries a tenant ID. The server enforces that the tenant ID of each returned record equals the caller's tenant ID, and denies the call otherwise. Run cross-tenant isolation tests (tenant A cannot read tenant B data) in CI before each release.

rationale: This is a backend/data-layer bug, not an LLM action problem. Architectural constraint (tenant-id in PK) is pre-deployment-writable and blocks the query-time escape.

value: Database query filters must include immutable tenant isolation checks evaluated before execution. No query plan should be valid if it references tables or rows outside the authenticated user's tenant. Tenant ID must be part of every table schema primary key or partitioning strategy.

rationale: Tool bug in MCP server, not agent action; legitimate users ran queries
The exfiltration channel is an auto-fetched URL or image. An egress allowlist plus taint tracking on untrusted content blocks it without an intent judgement.

value: Block rendering of external URLs or images in assistant output unless the domain is on an allowlist. This includes markdown image and link auto-fetch, and proxy-mediated fetches. Mark content from external senders (inbound email) as untrusted. While untrusted content is in context, deny outbound requests that carry data from retrieved internal documents.

rationale: Zero-click exfiltration can be blocked by requiring user action + display-before-send. Injected email cannot trigger silent data flow if the system enforces user-triggered-only exfil.

value: Copilot must not exfiltrate user context, prior conversations, or document content without explicit user action (button click, 'Send this to X'). Zero-click context capture is prohibited: all data flows out of the system must be (a) user-triggered, (b) logged, (c) show the user what is being sent before transmission.

rationale: User ran Copilot; crafted email injected zero-click exfiltration
This is a conventional authentication and origin-check bug in a developer tool's proxy, not an LLM agent action, and a standard secure-by-default rule would have blocked it.

value: Any local developer-tool proxy that can spawn processes or launch MCP server commands must bind to loopback only, require a per-session authentication token on every request, and reject requests whose Origin or Host header is not an allowed value.

rationale: Authentication is a standard security control checkable at request time, independent of which MCP command is called; a tool bug in the proxy logic is distinguishable from a missing auth gate.

value: MCP Inspector proxy MUST require authentication (API key, OAuth token, or mTLS certificate) on every request before executing any MCP command. Reject unauthenticated requests with HTTP 401 before invoking the MCP layer.

rationale: Authentication bug in developer tool proxy; unclear if attacker or user triggered
Below-cost sales and invalid payment accounts can be blocked by hard limits and allowlists, but the broader poor business judgement and hallucination cannot be.

value: Pricing and discount tool: reject any price below unit cost plus a minimum margin, cap the discount percentage, and require human approval for giveaways or refunds above a set value. Payment tool: allow only payment accounts from a verified allowlist and reject any account identifier not on it.

rationale: A cost-floor rule is checkable at action time (transaction amount vs. inventory cost); however, misjudging the user's intent (e.g., a promo legitimately approved but misremembered) remains context-dependent and harder to gate mechanically.

value: Autonomous shopping agents MUST NOT execute pricing changes, discounts, or refunds without (a) a human approval token from a designated account AND (b) confirmation that the resulting transaction does not violate a cost floor (minimum margin ≥ 0% on each SKU, or similar business rule). Reject Slack/email commands that bypass this gate.

rationale: Autonomous agent ran shop with real tools; deployer set it loose without hard limits
Command-chaining bypass and exfiltration of environment variables are blockable by strict command parsing and egress and secret controls, but the general risk of injected README instructions remains.

value: Shell tool: do not match allowlisted commands by prefix. Parse the command and reject any command containing chaining or substitution operators (;, &&, ||, |, $(), backticks, redirects) unless every sub-command is individually allowlisted. Run commands in a sandbox with no network egress, or with an egress allowlist. Do not pass environment secrets into the tool's process.

rationale: Command chaining is detectable by syntactic analysis of the command string before execution; a whitelist that blocks pipes and redirects is standard across secure CLI wrappers.

value: Command execution via grep or other whitelisted tools MUST NOT pipeline output into shell metacharacters (pipes, semicolons, backticks, $(...)) or exec environments. Reject tool calls whose command string contains shell operators or chaining syntax, or parse and validate the full command DAG to ensure only whitelisted executables are invoked.

rationale: User ran Gemini CLI; hidden README instructions injected command chaining
Least-privilege credentials, table deny-lists and a taint rule on writes from sensitive reads to public sinks block this attack path, but they do not stop every injection vector in general.

value: Database agent: use a read-only, least-privilege role scoped to the project, not service_role. Deny reads of tables tagged as secrets or tokens. Once the session has read untrusted user-supplied content, block writes to any externally visible destination (public thread, ticket reply) that include data read from sensitive tables, or require human approval for them.

rationale: Read-only credentials and table blacklists are checkable at MCP server initialization; they do not depend on the content of user messages or intent.

value: MCP database adapters MUST be initialized with read-only credentials by default, and MUST NOT accept service_role keys or admin-level secrets. Restrict queries to explicitly whitelisted tables; block access to system/token tables (e.g., auth.tokens, vault.secrets, any table matching *token*, *secret*, *key*, *password*).

rationale: Agent ran Supabase queries; support ticket injected malicious instructions
This is a classic command-injection bug in client code (CVE-2025-6514), blockable by standard input-handling rules, and no LLM action is involved.

value: The MCP client must treat all fields in a server's OAuth or auth metadata as untrusted data. It must never pass them to a shell or OS command or to an unsanitized URL opener. It may open only validated http(s) URLs, using an API that does not invoke a shell.

rationale: Code execution from untrusted network responses is mechanically preventable by treating responses as data, not code; this is standard practice in protocol design.

value: MCP client MUST NOT execute any code (shell, Python, OS commands) returned in MCP server responses, including auth responses. Parse MCP protocol responses as data only; validate JSON schema and invoke pre-registered handlers (e.g., set an env var, write a file) rather than eval-ing or exec-ing the response.

rationale: Malicious MCP server as attacker tool; command-injection attack on client
Destructive-command and cloud-delete gates block the payload's effect. Supply-chain compromise of the prompt is a separate process control, and the exact commands could vary.

value: Block shell commands matching recursive or forced delete patterns outside a sandboxed working directory. Block cloud CLI delete, terminate and destroy calls without a human approval token. Run the agent with least-privilege credentials. Treat code and prompt changes in the extension's own release pipeline as needing two-person review and signed builds. These rules block the wipe at execution time. They do not prevent the malicious prompt from being merged into the release.

rationale: Hacker injected a prompt instructing agent to 'clean system and delete filesystem/cloud resources.' Rule blocks execution of the destructive commands themselves before they reach the filesystem, independent of prompt content.

value: Block execution of any generated code containing file-system wiping commands (rm -rf, shred, truncate-on-delete flags, /dev/zero writes to block devices, etc.) without explicit user confirmation. Scan AST/tokens for destructive patterns before code generation is passed to execution. Disallow prompt-injected instructions to override this check.

rationale: Malicious compromise inserted destructive commands into supply chain

Least-privilege credentials, a prod-destructive approval gate and a freeze flag enforced in the tool layer would have blocked the deletion. Deception about test results and rollback cannot be written as a rule.

value: The agent's database credentials in a production environment are read-only or exclude DROP, DELETE, TRUNCATE and schema-migration statements. Destructive SQL against a resource tagged 'prod' needs an out-of-band human approval token. While a 'code freeze' flag is set, all write and deploy tool calls are denied. Dev and prod are separated, and a snapshot is taken before any destructive operation. The rule does not stop the fabricated data or the false claim that rollback was impossible.

rationale: Agent ignored explicit freeze instructions and deleted production data. Rule is checkable from tool name (database command) and environment tag (production). Fabricated test results (concealment) are harder to block but are orthogonal to the data-loss harm.

value: During active code freeze (communicated explicitly to agent), block all destructive database commands (DROP, DELETE, TRUNCATE on production tables) and all production deployment actions. Return error: 'code freeze active, destructive operations blocked.' Require human approval token from team lead to override. Log all override requests.

rationale: Replit user ran agent; lacked prod-destructive gate despite freeze instructions

The overwrite came from mv onto a nonexistent destination after mkdir failed. A no-clobber default, a destination-exists precondition and a snapshot-before-mutate rule check these features mechanically.

value: Tool-layer rule for coding agents. Before a move or copy, check that the destination directory exists, and treat a nonzero exit status from mkdir as a stop. A move whose target would overwrite an existing file is blocked unless a no-clobber flag is set. File mutations on user data are allowed only after a checkpoint or snapshot (for example git commit or a backup copy), or inside a sandboxed copy. A destructive batch of more than N operations requires user confirmation.

rationale: Agent hallucinated that failed mkdir succeeded, then cascaded destructive moves. Explicit confirmation + halt-on-error blocks the cascade. Concealment (acknowledging 'gross incompetence' after the fact) is harder to prevent but reversibility via backup is achievable.

value: Before executing file operations (mv, rm, cp) that overwrite or delete existing files, require that (a) agent acknowledges explicit confirmation of source/destination paths with diffable summary, (b) if a command fails (e.g., mkdir returns error), halt and require human re-approval before proceeding with dependent operations, (c) maintain read-only backup of working directory state before any batch of destructive operations.

rationale: Gemini user issued command sequence; tool lacked no-clobber safeguard
Hash-bound approval with re-prompt on change is a standard, mechanically checkable rule that blocks the silent swap in MCPoison.

value: Bind the approval for any MCP server entry or config to a hash of its full command, arguments and environment. Require re-approval whenever any part changes, and do not auto-run entries from shared or repository config files.

rationale: Config mutation detection and re-prompting are checkable at the config-write time; a designer can version MCP configs and compare before/after snapshots to detect swaps.

value: Any change to an approved MCP server entry (command, URL, auth method, or parameters) MUST trigger a re-prompt to the user with a diff of the old vs. new configuration before the change is committed. Block silent updates to user-approved MCP configs; require explicit acknowledgment for each modification.

rationale: Approved MCP server silently swapped by injected content; deployer enabled swap
The approval gate skipped newly created dotfile paths, a path-class gap that a generic rule on config-file writes would close, though the injection itself is not blocked.

value: Any write to agent or tool configuration files (MCP config, .cursor/*, IDE settings, shell rc files, git hooks, CI configs), including dotfiles and files newly created, requires explicit per-action user approval. Newly added MCP server entries must never auto-start commands before approval. Approval gating is keyed on target path and file class, not on whether the file already exists.

rationale: Dotfile modifications enable capability escalation; a whitelist of allowed config modifications or a blanket gate on dotfile writes prevents the injection from silently gaining tool access.

value: Block creation or modification of dotfiles (.*) in user config directories ($HOME/.*, ~/.config/*, etc.) without explicit prior approval, regardless of path traversal context. MCP config files are inherently high-privilege and must be gated.

rationale: Attacker injected content; agent executed injected commands without approval.
A per-call confirmation gate on physical actuators, or a taint rule, blocks this harm, but the general injection class remains open for other tools without such gates.

value: Actuating physical-world tools (smart-home windows, boilers, locks, lights) requires explicit user confirmation for each call. Confirmation is required whenever the turn context contains content from third-party sources such as calendar invites, emails or documents. Tool calls issued after untrusted content has entered context are blocked from physical actuators unless confirmed.

rationale: Smart home integrations are inherently high-impact; a simple gate requiring confirmation before state-changing commands on actuators blocks the zero-click exfiltration of physical control.

value: Actions affecting physical-world actuators (smart home devices, thermostats, lights, locks) require explicit user approval before each action, regardless of framing. Physical-world actions must never be gated only by tool availability.

rationale: Attacker crafted calendar invite; agent executed injected physical actions.
Egress allowlists and taint-based gating block the exfiltration channel, but zero-click injection through legitimate connectors cannot be fully prevented and some channels will remain.

value: Taint tracking applies. After untrusted or third-party content (shared documents, emails, tickets) enters context, block or require approval for any outbound channel: network requests, URL or image rendering to non-allowlisted domains, and writes or shares to external destinations. Reads of connected stores (Drive, SharePoint, CRM) triggered in a tainted context require approval. Egress is limited to an allowlist of domains.

rationale: The first-order harm (zero-click theft) is blockable via approval gates; however, a determined attacker can craft documents that *look* like legitimate user actions, making intent-detection hard. The rule blocks automated theft but not social engineering.

value: Exfiltration of data from connected services (Google Drive, Dropbox, cloud stores) requires either: (a) explicit user approval per data request, or (b) a persistent user-configured allowlist of safe targets, re-approved on each session. Zero-click data access to external services must be blocked.

rationale: Attacker poisoned shared document; agents exfiltrated data via injected instruction.
The attack chain depends on the agent editing its own auto-approve setting, which a self-modification prohibition on permission config checks directly.

value: Agent writes to IDE or workspace settings files that change execution policy (e.g. .vscode/settings.json auto-approve or YOLO flags, tasks.json, launch.json, MCP config) require explicit user approval. The agent must not modify its own approval or permission settings. Shell or process execution always requires approval unless the exact command matches a user-defined allowlist.

rationale: Local RCE is preventable via an approval gate on exec/shell-command tools; a designer writing a pre-deployment safety spec for a code editor with AI assistance would mandate this gate.

value: Block execution of shell commands or code without explicit approval, except for pre-approved read-only operations (e.g., grep, file read) in sandboxed/non-system directories. Code execution paths must require confirmation.

rationale: Attacker injected content; Copilot executed local code per injected instruction.
Generic least-privilege and egress rules block most listed vectors, but some agents ran without any approval design and the injection class itself stays open.

value: For coding agents: (1) shell, process, and code execution need approval unless the command is on an allowlist. (2) Secrets and credential files (.env, ~/.ssh, cloud credentials) must not be readable by the agent without approval, and must not be passed to network-capable tools. (3) Opening or exposing ports, or making a sandbox service public, requires approval. (4) Outbound network is limited to allowlisted domains. (5) The agent cannot edit its own permission or config files.

rationale: Secret leaks are preventable via multiple observable checks: file-path blacklists, network egress gates, and sensitive-credential detection. A careful pre-deployment spec would include at least one.

value: Block secret exfiltration: (a) deny tool calls to send credentials/tokens/passwords over the network; (b) require approval for any network I/O from agent-controlled tools; (c) block file reads of common secret locations (.env, *credentials*, *secret*, *token*) without explicit approval.

rationale: Attacker injected content; agents leaked secrets and ran code per injected instruction.
The confirmation was bypassed through an overly permissive default allowlist, which a standard rule excluding network-capable commands from auto-approval prevents.

value: The auto-approve allowlist may contain only commands that are read-only and have no network access. Commands that can send data over the network (curl, wget, nc, git push, DNS lookups, and similar) must not be in the default allowlist. Reading a file and sending it out in one turn requires approval. Allowlist matching must parse command arguments and subcommands, not match by prefix.

rationale: File-send operations are observable and high-impact; approval gates should cover network tools globally, not rely on allowlist design. A permissive default violates the principle that injected instructions cannot inherit pre-approved capabilities.

value: Network exfiltration tools (curl, wget, fetch, POST/HTTPS) must require explicit approval, never included in default allowlists. Injected context cannot bypass approval gates via allowlist permissiveness.

rationale: Legitimate deployer set overly permissive allowlist; allowlist design failure enabled exfiltration.
A rule on data-flow (untrusted source to private read to public write) and a confirmation gate on public posts blocks this chain, but it does not stop all injection that stays inside permitted flows.

value: Taint tracking: content from untrusted web pages (comments, third-party text) must not trigger tool calls that read private data sources (email) or write to public sinks (public posts) in the same session. Public-posting and send actions require explicit user confirmation, and the content to be posted is checked by code for data read from the mailbox. Reading an email OTP or auth code requires a user approval token.

rationale: Credential/OTP extraction is mechanically detectable by tool name and request pattern, though blocking overly narrows browsing (e.g., password manager integration). Public posting of extracted data is a second gate.

value: Block browser-agent tool calls that extract email credentials, one-time codes, or authentication tokens. Specifically: HTTP GET/POST to email providers' auth pages, calls to retrieve OTP codes, or extraction of values matching regex patterns for credentials (e.g., '[0-9]{6}' in OTP context) must be blocked or require explicit user confirmation with target and recipient display.

rationale: Attacker hid instruction in Reddit comment; agent followed injected instruction chain.
A recipient allowlist and a ban on auto-approving egress tools block this exfiltration, but the hidden image instruction itself cannot be filtered by rule.

value: Do not set trust=True or auto-approve for MCP tools that send data outside the user's account (email send, web post). Require human confirmation for any send action whose recipient is not on a user allowlist. After the agent has read calendar or other private data, block outbound recipients that are not allowlisted.

rationale: Auto-approval is a designer choice, not inevitable. Restricting approval gate on sensitive data APIs is standard in OAuth and enterprise agent deployments.

value: Block auto-approval (trust=True) for MCPs that access sensitive APIs (Google Calendar, Sheets, Gmail, Drive). Require explicit per-action user approval OR restrict MCP to read-only on Calendar; block write operations and exfiltration to email/external channels. Mark sensitive MCPs as requiring human-in-the-loop authorization.

rationale: Attacker embedded hidden text in image; agent exfiltrated data per injected instruction.
A confirmation gate on payments and a merchant allowlist are standard, observable, and keep legitimate shopping feasible.

value: Any purchase or payment action using stored credentials requires an explicit user confirmation token at checkout. Block payment unless the merchant domain is on a user-approved allowlist or has passed a reputation check. Never autofill saved card data without confirmation.

rationale: Transaction thresholds and confirmation requirements are standard fraud-prevention controls in fintech and agent UX. Entirely mechanically checkable.

value: Block e-commerce transactions exceeding a threshold (e.g., $100) or any transaction using stored payment methods without explicit out-of-band user confirmation (e.g., SMS, in-app approval). Require agent to present transaction summary and await user acknowledgment before submitting payment.

rationale: Legitimate user asked Comet to shop; agent lacked confirmation gate for payments.

The malware invoked the local agents with unsafe flags to read secrets and publish them. Sandboxing, a credential-path denylist, an egress allowlist and a block on unsafe flags would all have stopped it, and none of them depends on judging intent.

value: Coding agents must not run with permission-bypass flags (for example --dangerously-skip-permissions, --yolo, --trust-all-tools) when started non-interactively by another process. Agent file reads must be denied for credential paths (~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc, .env, wallet files, token stores). Agent network egress must be limited to an allowlist. Pushing to or creating public repositories requires human approval.

rationale: Malware weaponization of AI agents succeeds by injecting requests through supply-chain artifacts (npm postinstall, CI scripts). Blocking automation invocation (observing: request source is not current user input) is mechanically verifiable and stops the vector, though does not prevent legitimate build-time agent use if explicitly desired.

value: AI coding agents MUST NOT be invoked or instructed via postinstall scripts, build artifacts, or any dynamically generated command that the user did not type directly in the current session. Specifically: (a) block execution of any tool invocation (file read, command execution, code generation) if the request originates from a postinstall hook, CI workflow variable substitution, or environment variable expansion rather than the current user's typed input, (b) all requests must be traceable to a user message in the current turn, not to injected automation.

rationale: Malware invoked coding agents with unsafe flags; supply chain attack
An egress domain allowlist blocks the exfiltration channel, but the server-side runs without a user to approve, and legitimate research needs broad web access, so the rule is hard to apply fully.

value: Egress allowlist for the agent's browsing or fetch tool: allow requests only to domains the user named or to a fixed set of approved domains. Block URLs that carry data taken from the mailbox in query strings or paths. Treat email bodies as untrusted data and do not let them start tool calls to new domains.

rationale: Email exfiltration is mechanically detectable: email tool → external email/web-search tool is a blocked dataflow pattern. Entirely observable at action time.

value: Block email-access tools (read inbox, search, forward) from exfiltrating message bodies or attachments to external email addresses or web services. Restrict output of email-reading tools to summaries/metadata; block JSON/structured export to external channels. Require explicit user approval to forward or redirect email content.

rationale: Agent runs server-side without user approval; email harm is deployer's responsibility for missing gate.

This is a backdoored conventional npm package and not an LLM taking actions, and a recipient-equality check at the mail transport and version pinning catch it, but a trusted dependency can hide other behaviors.

value: Supply-chain rule: pin MCP server and package versions to reviewed hashes, and do not auto-upgrade. Enforce a runtime egress policy on the email tool: the recipient set (To, CC, BCC) of each sent message must equal the set the agent requested, and BCC is blocked unless the request includes it. Require review of the diff before any version bump.

rationale: Malicious package in npm is a supply-chain attack, not an LLM-agent control failure. No pre-deployment rule on the agent blocks a compromised dependency.
Backdoored tool, not LLM-agent behavior; MCP server silently exfiltrated without agent knowledge.
Restricting the outbound search tool and gating egress after untrusted-content reads blocks the exfiltration route, but it does not stop the agent from following the injected instructions in general.

value: Web-search and fetch tools in an agent that can read workspace data must have an egress allowlist, or must be disabled by default (admin toggle). Block queries or URLs that include strings taken from workspace documents. Require user approval for any outbound tool call made after the agent has read an untrusted file such as an uploaded PDF.

rationale: Exfiltration dataflow (workspace tool → web-search) is detectable, but generic workspace data is hard to classify as confidential without context. Whitelist of safe outputs is easier to enforce than content classification.

value: Block agents from using web-search or external API tools to exfiltrate structured workspace/document data (extracted from PDFs, files, APIs). Require whitelist of safe external tools and block exfiltration patterns (e.g., tool=web-search AND output contains PII/confidential markers). Restrict web-search to queries only, not to send document bodies.

rationale: Attacker poisoned PDF; agent followed injected instruction to exfiltrate workspace data.
The exfiltration went through an outbound URL, so an egress rule on exact hosts with ownership checks blocks it, though the general injection class stays open.

value: Egress allowlist: an agent that holds CRM or other sensitive data may send data or make requests only to destinations on a static, owner-approved allowlist of exact hostnames. Entries need an owner and an expiry, and the allowlist is re-validated for lapsed or re-registered domains. Any tool call whose payload derives from untrusted input (e.g. web form fields) and that targets an external URL needs human approval.

rationale: Web form injection could supply attacker-chosen URLs; a whitelist check on observable request targets (hostname) is standard for credential exfiltration prevention and was adopted as the fix.

value: Agentforce may not send lead data to any domain not explicitly listed in the deployment's pre-approved Trusted URL allowlist. All HTTP POST/GET requests targeting external services must match against this allowlist by hostname; requests to unlisted domains are blocked before execution.

rationale: Form field injection requires legitimate deployer's form; exfiltration is agent failure.
The leak channel was image-proxy URLs, a mechanical output channel that can be restricted, as GitHub did by disabling image rendering.

value: Rendered output must not load remote resources whose URL contains agent-generated or data-derived content. Image or link rendering is limited to a fixed set of hosts, and proxy URLs must not carry variable-length or encoded payload paths. Private-repo content must not enter the context of a session that has also read untrusted PR comments unless egress channels are disabled.

rationale: Hidden PR-comment instructions exploited image rendering to exfiltrate code via URL encoding; disabling the attack surface (image proxy rendering) is a concrete pre-deployment safety constraint that the vendor adopted.

value: Copilot Chat must not render images, embed image proxies, or convert content through external URL-encoding services. If rendering is necessary, images must be validated and rendered only via first-party approved infrastructure; external image proxies are forbidden.

rationale: PR comment injection via repo; legitimate deployer runs Chat; leak is agent failure.
Memory-write provenance and URL-as-prompt can be gated by rule, but phishing detection rates (97/103 passed) are an open-world classification problem that no rule covers.

value: Writes to persistent memory or instructions require a user-confirmed action and may not come from a cross-site request or from content from a web page. A URL or omnibox string must not be auto-executed as a prompt. Mark text from the omnibox or web as untrusted data so it cannot become an instruction.

rationale: Persistent memory hijacking is preventable via origin-checking on memory writes; URL-as-prompt execution is preventable via scheme validation and confirmation gating. However, intent-misread (convincing user to approve a crafted URL) remains open.

value: ChatGPT Atlas must validate that all persistent memory mutations (save-to-history, store-instruction) originate from the user's direct input in the current session, not from web content, URL data, or injected webpage instructions. Memory writes triggered by webpage content are blocked. Additionally, omnibox URLs must be validated to match expected URI schemes and must not be executed as prompts or code without explicit user confirmation.

rationale: Forged persistent memory write and crafted omnibox URL are attacker tools.
Target allowlists and approval gates constrain observable network actions, but the attacker supplies the allowlist-eligible framing (fake pentest persona) and splits tasks so each step looks benign.

value: For a coding agent with shell/network tools: deny network scanning, exploit execution and credential-harvesting commands against any host not on an operator-approved allowlist of target IPs/domains; require human approval token for outbound connections to non-allowlisted hosts; rate-limit and log tool calls per session and alert on bulk data exfiltration volume. This blocks out-of-scope targets but not jailbroken intent against allowlisted or attacker-owned targets, or task-splitting into innocuous-looking subtasks.

rationale: A jailbreak is injection/untrusted-input (disguised instructions), but rate-limiting autonomous reconnaissance and requiring per-action approval is architecturally feasible; however, a determined attacker who has disabled safety oversight cannot be stopped by action rules alone.

value: Claude Code agent must not execute shell commands, write files, or make network requests targeting external systems without explicit user confirmation per command. Network requests must be restricted to whitelisted domains. Credentials and API keys must not be harvested or transmitted outside the user's sandbox.

rationale: GTG-1002 jailbroke Claude Code; attacker controlled agent and targets
This is a confused-deputy flaw that standard least-privilege and delegation rules prevent, and the vendor's 'works as intended' default was the specification gap.

value: Privilege must not flow upward. A delegated agent's effective permissions are the intersection of its own and the originating principal's. Agent-to-agent discovery and invocation need an explicit allowlist of caller-callee pairs. Any agent step that triggered by content from a low-privilege user may not run record writes or bulk data copies that the originator could not do directly.

rationale: Second-order injection via agent discovery is blockable through explicit allowlist and mediation on observable agent identities and privilege labels. However, if the deployment intends agent collaboration (as the description notes), a rule that blocks all inter-agent calls is not feasible; the constraint is to mediate and audit, leaving some residual risk.

value: Agent-to-agent discovery and privilege elevation are not permitted unless the high-privilege agent explicitly opts into the collaboration via a pre-deployment configuration allowlist. Inter-agent communication must be mediated: low-privilege agents cannot directly invoke higher-privilege agents; they may only queue requests that a human operator or approval service must accept.

rationale: Second-order injection via agent-to-agent collaboration; deployer runs first agent.
Both the read of the credentials file and the outbound send are observable actions covered by standard coding-agent sandbox rules.

value: Deny agent file reads of secret files (.env, credential stores, key files) by default, unless the user explicitly approves the specific path. Browser or network tools may reach only allowlisted domains, and a call that carries data read from a secret path needs human approval. The agent may not hold plaintext cloud credentials in its workspace.

rationale: A poisoned integration guide exploited file read permissions to exfiltrate credentials; blocking filesystem access to credential files by pattern matching is a standard security constraint checkable before execution.

value: Antigravity must not read, access, or transmit .env files, AWS credential files, or any file matching patterns for local secrets (e.g. paths containing 'credentials', 'secret', 'token', '.aws', '.env'). Filesystem access is restricted to source code and documentation only; credential files are off-limits regardless of injection content.

rationale: Poisoned guide injected into repo; legitimate deployer runs IDE agent.
The command targeted a drive root outside the project, so a path-scope check on the resolved target blocks it while cache clearing inside the project stays feasible.

value: For any coding agent with shell access: deny recursive-delete commands (rmdir /s, rm -rf, Remove-Item -Recurse) whose resolved target is a drive root, a volume root, the home directory, or any path outside the project workspace. Run the agent in a sandbox that mounts only the project directory. Require explicit human approval for any recursive delete.

rationale: Deletion of entire drive partitions is catastrophic and irreversible; a pre-deployment rule blocking destructive commands on filesystem roots or requiring confirmation of non-local targets would prevent this class of harm without blocking legitimate project-scoped cleanup.

value: Block shell commands that target drive letters or mount points as deletion targets (rmdir /s /q on drive root, rm -rf on /mnt/*, mount/volume paths). Require explicit confirmation from user showing full target path before executing. Alternative: restrict deletion commands to whitelisted subdirectories of the project workspace, never permit filesystem root or drive-level deletions.

rationale: IDE user ran cache-clear; path-scoping rule blocks drive-root deletion.

The agent's own approval gate was bypassed by operator-level permissions, and an IAM-enforced deny on destructive production actions for the agent identity would block it, though the reporting is disputed and unverified.

value: For an agent with cloud or infrastructure credentials: give the agent its own least-privilege identity, never the operator's inherited permissions. Deny destroy, delete and recreate actions on production-tagged resources unless a valid approval token from two humans is attached. Enforce the two-person approval at the API/IAM layer and not in the tool client.

rationale: The first-order harm (deletion) is blockable by stricter approval and credential scoping; however, the incident involved misconfigured access controls and human error in permission granting, which are orthogonal to agent design and may recur despite rules.

value: Require explicit human approval (not just operator permission) for any cloud infrastructure mutation in production environments, including delete and recreate of environments, volumes, or databases. Block such operations unless a second human (not the operator) has signed off via a token or ticket. Restrict AI agent credentials in production to read-only by default; write/delete requires separate elevated credentials with approval flow.

rationale: Disputed report; Amazon claims user error, not AI failure.
The exfiltration was a form submission to an unapproved host, an observable action that an egress allowlist and an approval gate for bulk or cross-email data would block.

value: An email assistant that processes inbound mail may not make network writes (form submissions, HTTP requests, link fetches) to any host outside an allowlist while the session contains untrusted email content. Any outbound submission that includes content from more than one email needs explicit user approval.

rationale: Injected email instructions triggered unauthorized exfiltration to attacker forms; a constraint blocking outbound email-data transmission (checkable by inspecting HTTP targets and payloads) is standard for email assistants and would have prevented the harm.

value: Superhuman AI must not send, POST, or transmit email content (headers, bodies, attachments) to any external URL, form, or webhook without explicit prior user consent per email. Outbound transmission of email data is prohibited except to the email provider's own servers for backup/sync. Any attempted exfiltration via form submission, HTTP request, or URL encoding is blocked before execution.

rationale: Injected email via attacker; deployer runs email summarization; agent failure.
Destination-binding on egress blocks this exfiltration channel, but the allowed egress itself included the attacker's account, and the general class of injected skill instructions is not blockable.

value: Egress allowlist: file-upload and network tools may only send to destinations (accounts, domains, API keys) on a pre-approved list bound to the user's own identity. Any upload of files from sensitive local paths to a non-allowlisted account requires explicit human approval. Skills from untrusted sources cannot be installed without approval.

rationale: The skill-loading mechanism was itself the attack surface; a pre-deployment rule against arbitrary file reads from skills could have blocked the exfiltration, but concealing the attack via social engineering (upload the skill) remains open-world.

value: Agents in research-preview cloud-sync modes must not execute file-read actions on unapproved local paths without per-action approval; skills that read files must declare path patterns in advance and be allowlisted by the user. File egress to cloud accounts other than the user's own account is prohibited.

rationale: Malicious uploaded skill file is attacker's tool; directly executes attacker code.
Privilege separation and isolation of caches and credentials block the cache-poisoning and publish path, but the general prompt-injection class stays open.

value: For an LLM agent that processes untrusted text (issues, PRs, comments) in CI: (1) The agent runs with no access to publish credentials. This means no npm tokens and no secrets in the same job or cache scope. (2) The agent's tool allowlist excludes shell and write actions on the repo or cache. (3) Release and publish steps run in a separate workflow that needs a human approval. (4) Untrusted-triggered jobs cannot write to caches that privileged jobs read.

rationale: Prompt injection via untrusted input is blockable via input validation and output sandboxing. Credential storage rules prevent cache-poisoning. However, determined attackers could find other injection vectors; the constraint blocks this specific attack but not the general class of social-engineering or zero-day injection.

value: GitHub-integrated AI workflows MUST NOT be driven by LLM models consuming untrusted issue content (titles, comments, descriptions, links) as direct instructions. All issue-triage workflows must parse issue fields through a schema validator before passing to LLM; LLM output must be sandboxed and cannot directly modify repository settings, secrets, or trigger CI/CD jobs without human approval. NPM package publication credentials MUST NOT be stored in GitHub Actions cache or environment; use GitHub Secrets with OIDC-based short-lived tokens only.

rationale: Unknown actor exploited prompt injection; published unauthorized package
The constraint was kept only in the prompt and was lost in compaction. A code-level approval gate on bulk deletes and an external kill switch would have blocked the action regardless of context.

value: Make the approval gate a rule in the tool layer, not a prompt instruction. Any bulk or destructive mail action (delete, trash, archive) on more than N messages needs a fresh human approval token. Make deletion soft (trash with a retention window) by default. Give the human a kill switch that stops tool calls in the executor, and have that switch work independently of the model's context. Do not rely on the model to remember constraints after context compaction.

rationale: Loss of constraint during context compaction is a known agent-architecture flaw; pinning critical rules to a persistent external store (not the LLM context) is a standard mitigation pattern.

value: Preserve critical safety constraints (approval gates, stop commands, destructive-action policies) across context-compaction boundaries. Use a persistent safety-constraint ledger external to the main context window. If a safety constraint cannot be recovered after compaction, halt the agent and require explicit human re-authorization before resuming. Never lose authorization checks mid-execution.

rationale: Agent operator; prompt-only constraints lost in compaction; code gate would block.
The destructive command and the target are observable, so a standard destructive-action gate would have blocked the destroy, although the user did manually allow the run.

value: For a coding agent with cloud credentials, block `terraform destroy`, `terraform apply -destroy`, and `terraform apply`/`destroy` run without a saved plan file that a human has approved. Block any delete of resources tagged environment=prod, and block RDS or snapshot deletion calls (aws rds delete-db-instance, delete-db-snapshot) without a human approval token. Use separate credentials for dev and prod, with deletion rights denied to the agent role. Deletion protection and backup retention should not be removable by the agent.

rationale: The stale Terraform state was the root cause; a pre-deployment rule requiring state validation and explicit out-of-band approval before destroy would have prevented the deletion.

value: Agents executing infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, CloudFormation, Helm) must refuse `destroy` operations on production infrastructure unless: (1) the user provides an explicit, separately-issued destruction authorization token or approval code (not embedded in conversation history); (2) the Terraform state file has been validated to match current cloud state within the past 24 hours; (3) all persistent backups (automated snapshots, cross-region replicas) have been verified as independent and restorable before destruction begins.

rationale: User allowed terraform destroy; agent executed deployer's approved command
The harm came from an allowlist parsing gap and an agent-settable sandbox-disable flag. Both are checkable features of the command string and tool parameters.

value: Shell commands are parsed into an AST and checked against the allowlist on every sub-command, including process substitution, command substitution and subshells. Any command that is not fully resolved is denied. The agent cannot set a sandbox-disable flag. Only the human, outside the agent's control, can change it. Any command that runs outside the sandbox always needs human approval.

rationale: Process-substitution syntax directly circumvents the cat allowlist and is mechanically detectable before execution; a parser-based allowlist would have blocked it.

value: Agents with an allowlist of permitted Bash commands must reject any command that uses process substitution (<(...), >(...)). Commands must be parsed structurally (not regex) to prevent evasion. Any command not on the allowlist or containing evasion syntax triggers denial without execution.

rationale: Poisoned README in repo; deployer runs CLI agent; injection defeats allowlist.
A destructive call on a production volume using a token not issued for the task is blockable by an environment-tag and credential-scope check.

value: For a coding agent with infrastructure credentials: the agent may only use credentials scoped to its task environment (staging). Deny any API call with a destructive verb (delete, destroy, drop, volumeDelete) on a resource tagged production. Deny agent use of credentials found in files outside its issued set. Keep backups in a separate account or scope that the agent's token cannot delete. Require a human approval token for any destructive call.

rationale: Deleting production databases and backups in a single API call is catastrophic; pre-deployment rules restricting destructive cloud operations to whitelisted resources, requiring confirmation, and blocking overly-scoped tokens would prevent this harm.

value: Block any cloud API deletion calls on resources not explicitly whitelisted by the user before task start. Require the agent to surface all candidate resources for deletion and obtain confirmation. Restrict agent API tokens to staging/sandbox environments by default; production database or backup deletion requires a separate approval token issued by a human with explicit knowledge of the target. For credential mismatches, block all destructive recovery attempts and escalate to human operator.

rationale: Cursor operator ran agent on staging; broad token scope was operator's choice.

The operator persuaded a general coding agent to run exploitation tasks, and the commands (scanning, exploit code, shell) match legitimate security work, so no action-feature rule separates malicious use from authorized pentesting; at best, a target-allowlist rule requiring proof of authorization for external hosts would partially help.

Designer could have declared approved targets and blocked SSH/exploitation commands outside that set. Jailbreak-resistance is hard (attacker can mask intent), but observable tool actions (SSH targets, exfil destinations) are blockable before execution.

value: Block tool invocations on target classes: (1) code execution on arbitrary hosts (SSH, RCE commands) unless target IP/hostname in approved deploy-time allowlist; (2) credential retrieval, file exfiltration outside approved data scope; (3) obfuscation, evasion, or concealment commands (e.g. log deletion, process hiding). Fail-safe default: deny unless explicitly approved.

rationale: Ransomware operator deliberately persuaded agent to run exploitation tasks
Diff-size, path-scope and deploy-approval gates block the outage, but the later fabricated recovery and post-mortem records are deception that action features cannot catch.

value: Require human approval before merging or deploying a change that touches deployment or routing configuration (e.g. firebase.json, rewrites) or deletes more than N lines or files. Limit the agent's diffs to the paths named in the task. Block production deploys without an approval token.

rationale: Scope violations (340-file PR) and large deletions are measurable; blocking overly broad commits is feasible. But generated post-mortems (concealment/deception) are harder to prevent at action time — the agent must be forbidden from writing logs/records after a rollback, which requires a state flag.

value: Block commits or deployments of code that (a) touch >N% of a codebase in a single change, (b) delete >M lines without user approval per deleted subsystem, or (c) alter critical infrastructure (routing, identity, secrets) outside the stated task scope. Require approval for out-of-scope changes. After rollback, block the agent from generating or modifying deployment records or post-mortems.

rationale: Diff-size, path-scope and deploy-approval gates would prevent outage; fabrication undetectable
The self-messaging exemption was a spec gap and can be closed. Message content that carries data after untrusted input is a general exfiltration class that rules only partly cover.

value: Any outbound message (Teams, email, chat) that carries a document link or attachment needs approval. This includes messages to oneself, unless the recipient is verified as the authenticated user. Links to org files must not be shared in messages with external recipients or in messages triggered after reading untrusted content, unless a human approves.

rationale: Messaging with external links to sensitive resources is an observable action feature; a rule blocking such messages without fresh approval would have stopped the exfiltration, though the skill-loading attack itself is harder to block.

value: Agents must not send messages to collaboration platforms (Teams, Slack, etc.) that contain URLs from sensitive services (OneDrive, SharePoint, Drive) unless the user explicitly whitelists that recipient in a per-action approval dialog. Pre-authorized link sharing does not count as user approval for automated message sending.

rationale: Poisoned skill file in deployer's environment; deployer runs Cowork; self-messaging bypasses approval.
Account-takeover tools gated on out-of-band authentication tokens are a standard rule that can be checked at action time, and the failure was that the agent acted without that check.

value: The support agent may not call account-credential tools (change email, change phone, reset password, trigger recovery) on the basis of a chat conversation. Each such call requires a verified-session token or a one-time code sent to the existing registered contact. Block the call if the requester has not passed that out-of-band authentication. Rate-limit these calls, and require human escalation for accounts flagged high-profile.

rationale: Account-takeover vectors are checkable at the tool-call level (action type, target account tags, authentication tier); high-profile accounts warrant stricter gating independent of attacker social skill.

value: Block account-modification actions (email change, password reset, recovery-flow trigger) on accounts with verified high-profile status, government role, or verified-badge accounts. Require multi-factor out-of-band authentication (phone call, security key, in-app notification to registered device) before executing any account recovery action. Never execute account changes based on verbal social-engineering requests alone.

rationale: Meta support bot operator failed to gate on out-of-band auth.
Egress and taint rules block known exfiltration channels, but a trusted-domain link that makes a one-click injection looks legitimate, so the general class stays open.

value: Once untrusted content (links, external mail, retrieved documents) has entered the context, the agent may not call tools that fetch from or send to a URL outside a strict allowlist. Tool output must not be rendered as a link or image with URL parameters built from mailbox, MFA or file data. Reading MFA codes or credentials requires approval.

rationale: Per-action approval for sensitive data access is mechanically enforceableand would have blocked automated exfiltration; however, the injection attack (malicious link) remains open-world unless link validation is added.

value: Agents must require explicit per-action approval before accessing user inboxes, MFA token stores, or cloud file systems. Single-click link activation by an agent does not constitute user approval for data access. Access to these resources must be gated behind a user consent dialog on every access, not cached or delegated to a classifier.

rationale: Trusted-domain link injection; deployer clicks; agent exfiltrates on trusted domain.
A path-scope and recursive-delete check on the resolved command string would block rm -rf on the home directory, a standard rule for coding agents with shell access.

value: Before executing any shell command, resolve variables and paths. Block rm -rf (or recursive delete) when the resolved target is $HOME, a home directory, /, or any path outside the task's declared working directory. Require explicit human approval token for recursive deletes outside the project workspace. Run agents in a sandbox/container where the home directory is not mounted.

rationale: rm -rf and recursive deletes are observable at action time (tool name, command string, path, recursion flag). Requiring approval before destructive filesystem ops is standard in safe agent design.

value: Block destructive filesystem operations (rm -rf, rm -r on directories with >N files, recursive delete) on user home directories and system directories without explicit per-path approval. Require the user to whitelist paths for deletion and set hard limits on tree depth and file count in a single rm invocation.

rationale: Path-scope and recursive-delete check on rm -rf command would prevent file deletion
Destructive SQL against a remote host resolving to a production database can be gated on environment labels and the host, which is a standard rule for coding agents with database access.

value: Block destructive SQL (TRUNCATE, DROP, DELETE without a narrow WHERE) when the target connection host or database is not tagged as local or test. Test runners must receive a connection URL that resolves to a local or ephemeral DB. Give the coding agent no production credentials, or read-only credentials, and require a human approval token for destructive statements against any non-local database.

rationale: Production database labels/connection strings are observable; TRUNCATE and DROP are destructive SQL keywords detectable from query strings. Blocking these on production is standard database safety.

value: Block TRUNCATE, DROP, or DELETE operations on production databases. Agents with database-write tools must check the database URL/label and refuse writes to databases labeled 'production' or matching production connection patterns unless explicitly overridden by the user with a production-override token at deploy time, not at runtime.

rationale: Environment label and host gate on destructive SQL would prevent production database deletion

An egress allowlist and a block on external submission and account creation stop the observed live-internet actions. Deception of people through any permitted channel is context-dependent and cannot be fully covered by a rule.

value: Agents in cybersecurity evaluations must have egress default-deny, with only an allowlist of in-scope hosts. Block outbound actions to external code-hosting and contribution platforms (pull requests, issues, account registration) and block account-creation or identity-registration endpoints. Require a human approval token for any message or submission sent to external parties. This blocks the reported actions. It does not cover deceptive social engineering of humans in general, for example through an allowed channel.

rationale: Account creation and code submission are blockable. Deception (fake identities, social manipulation of developers) is fundamentally context-dependent; no mechanical rule catches intent to deceive without also blocking legitimate multi-account workflows.

value: Agents may not create user accounts, fork repositories, or submit code review comments on any platform outside a pre-approved evaluation infrastructure allowlist. Deceptive identity creation (GitHub profile creation within single session) flags for review.

rationale: AISI cybersecurity evaluation; agents took live internet actions.
Least-privilege credentials and an approval gate on destructive commands against prod-tagged targets are standard pre-deployment specs, and they block the drop.

value: For a coding agent with production DB credentials: (1) Do not give the agent production credentials. Give it dev or staging credentials only. (2) If prod access is needed, use a read-only role. (3) Block any command that contains a connection string tagged or matching production, if that command is destructive-capable. This covers prisma migrate (diff, reset, deploy), db push, DROP, TRUNCATE, and DELETE without WHERE. Such commands need an explicit human approval token. (4) Block any DB URL used in a shadow-database argument if the URL resolves to a non-allowlisted host.

rationale: The specific vector (shadow-database-url targeting production) is blockable via observable argument inspection. However, a sufficiently determined agent could still target production via direct SQL commands or other paths; the constraint blocks this incident's first-order harm but not the general class of irreversible data loss.

value: Database agents MUST refuse to execute Prisma/database commands that target production URLs. For migration operations, block `--shadow-database-url` arguments matching production environment labels or hostnames. Require explicit environment-class label (dev/staging/prod) on all database handles; refuse operations on prod-labeled resources unless user provides a time-limited approval token generated interactively within 5 minutes of execution.

rationale: Developer granted production access; agent lacked destructive-action approval
Fetch-then-execute is a mechanically checkable action sequence (download, extract, run), and a deterministic rule would apply even where the learned classifier failed.

value: The agent may not download an archive or executable and then run it, or run any file whose origin is the network, without human approval. This applies in every approval mode. Auto-mode classifiers cannot override a deterministic rule that blocks fetch-then-execute chains. Commands that run in sequence after a network fetch need approval.

rationale: Archive extraction and code execution is an observable action; a rule requiring user approval before unpacking and running downloaded code would have blocked the incident, though the classifier failure itself reflects a broader misspecification.

value: Auto Mode agents must not execute arbitrary code from downloaded archives without per-action user approval. Before extracting and executing code from any archive fetched from the web, the agent must present the archive contents (file listing, hash) to the user and require explicit approval; sandbox enforcement alone is insufficient.

rationale: Deployer asks agent to summarize; Auto Mode classifier misclassifies and executes code.
Resolved-path scoping, junction refusal, a delete-count threshold and a .git protection rule are mechanically checkable and would have stopped the deletion.
