value: For coding agents with filesystem delete access: before any recursive delete (rm -rf, rmdir /s, Remove-Item -Recurse, shutil.rmtree), resolve real paths and refuse to traverse symlinks or junctions or reparse points. Deny deletes whose resolved target falls outside the declared task working directory, or that touch .git or any path tagged as live/original. Require explicit approval for deletions above N files. Run agents against copies with the originals mounted read-only or backed up.

rationale: Blocks junction-following by requiring symlink resolution and boundary check before delete. Rule is generic to any coding agent with filesystem access; it uses observable features (directory tags, presence of .git/, junction resolution) to prevent crossing into live project space. User authorized repair, but safety constraint prevents the specific mistake (following junctions out of sandbox).

value: Recursive delete, git reset --hard, or destructive filesystem operations on directories containing .git/ are blocked unless: (a) target directory is tagged as 'ephemeral-test' or 'sandbox', (b) working tree has uncommitted changes visible and user has approved deletion of all uncommitted work, (c) git object store will not be deleted. Windows junctions, symlinks, and mount points are resolved to their target and deletion is blocked if target is outside the designated working directory. Destructive operations log the full tree being deleted with file count before execution.

rationale: User authorized repair; agent followed junctions, deleted live files
A path-scoped deny or approval rule on recursive deletes blocks the loss. It leaves the task of freeing disk space feasible in scratch and cache directories.

value: Recursive delete (rm -rf or the equivalent) is allowed only inside a designated scratch or sandbox directory. Any recursive delete on a path outside it, or on a workspace root, a home directory or a drive root, needs human approval. Auto-execution of destructive commands stays off by default. Before a delete, the target size or file count must be checked, and a delete above a threshold needs approval.

rationale: Recursive deletion is mechanically detectable (command pattern, path depth) and irreversible; a rule blocking it from auto-execution without approval is standard practice and would have prevented the 120 GB loss.

value: Agents must not execute recursive delete operations (rm -rf, recursive wildcards on paths larger than the target, or operations spanning multiple directory levels) without explicit user approval of the specific path and confirmation of the intent. Terminal auto-execution mode must exclude recursive deletes.

rationale: Deployer asks agent to free disk space; autonomous misjudgement deletes client work.

Metadata-endpoint egress blocks, IMDSv2 and least-privilege roles are standard checkable controls that stop the credential theft, but the injection itself and misuse of legitimately granted permissions are not preventable by such rules.

value: For any agent runtime with tool or network access in a cloud account: (1) egress allowlist, so the agent's fetch/HTTP tools may not reach link-local or metadata addresses (169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254) or private ranges, and IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 is required or the metadata service is disabled; (2) the agent's execution role has least privilege, scoped to its own resources, with no wildcard access to other agents or secrets; (3) public-facing agents get no credentials that reach other agents or secrets. These rules block the credential theft and lateral reach. They do not stop the prompt injection that triggers the request, and they do not cover other abuse of the permissions the agent legitimately holds.

rationale: SSRF to credential metadata is a known attack surface; IMDSv2 token enforcement and metadata endpoint blocking are standard pre-deployment controls for any agent with AWS credentials, independent of this incident.

value: Block tool calls that target AWS metadata service endpoints (169.254.169.254, instance metadata URLs). Block HTTP requests without IMDSv2 token headers. Restrict agent credential exposure: credentials must not be injectable into tool call arguments or accessible via agent introspection; use short-lived scoped tokens per tool, not ambient credentials.

rationale: Legitimate deployer ran agent; harm was failure to gate injected content
Egress allowlists and an account-binding policy are standard for controlled systems, but the root cause was a human deployment choice and the facts are disputed and unclear.

value: Data-egress rule: for an agent connected to a classified or controlled-unclassified system, allow outbound network calls only to an approved destination allowlist. Block any outbound request to a non-approved domain. Block transmission of strings that match credential patterns or network-topology data. Block connecting an agent bound to a personal account to a controlled system. This does not cover the human decision to connect it, and the allegations are disputed.

rationale: A rule blocking transmission of credentials to third-party sites blocks this incident. The rule is checkable at action time (target domain and data content are observable), generic to any agent with access to sensitive data, and standard in defense/government security policies.

value: Agents may not send credentials, authentication tokens, API keys, or CUI-marked information to external third-party websites or services not explicitly listed in the task specification or deployment authorization. Agents must reject any outbound transmission of sensitive data to domains outside the organization's control. Exception: transmission to domains explicitly authorized in the task specification is permitted.

rationale: Human deployment choice disputed; facts unclear per Accenture
